After invoking others to unite in praise, the writer celebrates God's protecting and delivering care towards him, and then represents himself and the people of God as entering the sanctuary and uniting in solemn praise, with prayer for a continued blessing. Whether composed by David on his accession to power, or by some later writer in memory of the restoration from Babylon, its tone is joyful and trusting, and, in describing the fortune and destiny of the Jewish Church and its visible head, it is typically prophetical of the Christian Church and her greater and invisible Head.</title> <div sID="gen10518" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6855"/>1-4. After "now say" supply "give thanks."<div eID="gen10520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10521" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that his mercy--</hi>or, "for His mercy." <div eID="gen10521" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: PSALM 118 Psa 118:1-29 . After invoking others to unite in praise, the writer celebrates God's protecting and delivering care towards him, and then represents himself and the people of God as entering the sanctuary and uniting in solemn praise, with prayer for a continued blessing. Whether composed by David on his accession to power, or by some later writer in memory of the restoration from Babylon, its tone is joyful and trusting, and, in describing the fortune and destiny of the Jewish Church and its visible head, it is typically prophetical of the Christian Church and her greater and invisible Head. 1-4. The trine repetitions are emphatic (compare Psa 118:10-12, 15, 16; 115:12 , 13 ). Let ... say-- Oh! that Israel may say. now-- as in Psa 115:2 ; so in Psa 118:3 , 4 . After "now say" supply "give thanks." that his mercy-- or, "for His mercy."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6866"/><div sID="gen10533" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6866"/>22-23. These words are applied by Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.21.42">Mt 21:42</reference>) to Himself, as the foundation of the Church (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.4.11">Ac 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Ep 2:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.4">1Pe 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.7">7</reference>). It may here denote God's wondrous exaltation to power and influence of him whom the rulers of the nation despised. Whether (see on <reference osisRef="Ps.118.1">Psa 118:1</reference>) David or Zerubbabel (compare <reference osisRef="Hag.2.2">Hag 2:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.4.7-Zech.4.10">Zec 4:7-10</reference>) be primarily meant, there is here typically represented God's more wonderful doings in exalting Christ, crucified as an impostor, to be the Prince and Saviour and Head of His Church. <div eID="gen10533" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 22-23. These words are applied by Christ ( Mt 21:42 ) to Himself, as the foundation of the Church (compare Ac 4:11 ; Ep 2:20 ; 1Pe 2:4 , 7 ).
